page: Amazon Web Services r6a.large is an entry-level memory-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor. The hardware configuration consists of an AMD EPYC 7R13 x86_64 processor clocked at 3.6 GHz, delivering 2 vCPUs derived from a single physical core with multithreading enabled. The system is provisioned with 16 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, resulting in an 8 GB per vCPU ratio. The instance does not include integrated local storage or dedicated hardware accelerators, necessitating network-attached storage for local disk requirements.

Benchmark testing indicates strong single-core CPU throughput, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2,989.68 placing in the top quartile. However, the limited physical core count restricts aggregate parallel processing, keeping overall multi-core compute, software compilation, and database operation scores in the lower performance brackets. Memory bandwidth under large-block reads and writes registers at 31.33 GB/sec and 21.46 GB/sec respectively, alongside a 1 Gbps baseline network throughput.

From an architectural efficiency perspective, r6a.large delivers an economical entry point for memory-heavy environments that do not require high concurrent CPU capacity. The absence of bundled local storage and modest network bandwidth define its operational boundaries. The configuration is primarily suited for lightweight relational databases, small in-memory caching nodes, staging environments, and memory-bound background tasks.
description: Amazon Web Services r6a.large is a memory-optimized cloud server built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor and powered by an AMD EPYC 7R13 processor. It features 2 vCPUs spanning a single physical core, clocked at 3.6 GHz, paired with 16 GB of DDR4 memory at 3 GHz, providing a generous 8:1 memory-to-core ratio. The server lacks local storage and dedicated GPUs, relying on external network-attached volumes and operating on a 1 Gbps baseline network. In performance testing, the instance exhibits strong single-core CPU throughput in stress-ng evaluations, but multi-core processing, code compilation, and database operations rank lower due to limited core density. The r6a.large offers a cost-effective memory footprint for modest workloads requiring disproportionate RAM, including light in-memory caching, small relational database instances, and general memory-bound backend services.
